# Breakdown Diagnosis

A machine is down. Every minute it stays down, the plant is not producing — and
**the largest component of MTTR is usually not the repair, it is working out what
is wrong.**

The technician has five sources of evidence available and time to assemble none
of them. That gap is this skill.

**Quick start**

```
→ Capture the event: asset, time down, symptom, fault codes
→ SAFETY FIRST: if there is a safety implication, that leads. Always
→ Pull the sensor window; read shapes, not just threshold breaches
→ Mine maintenance history and the free-text close-out notes
→ Read the photos; consult the manual's troubleshooting tree
→ Rank candidate causes: evidence, cheapest discriminating test, expected fix
→ Cite the specific prior work orders behind each candidate
→ Draft the PM interval change that would stop it recurring
→ Emit the downtime record for the next production report
```

---

## Safety leads. Always.

**Where a failure has a safety implication, surface it first — before any
diagnosis.** Never let a diagnostic suggestion precede a safety flag.

**Every diagnosis opens with this line, flagged or not:** *"Follow your plant's
lockout procedure before anyone works on this machine. This is not a safety
assessment."* A false flag never removes it, and no step sends anyone to the
machine above it.

A technician reading a ranked list of likely causes is already reaching for
tools. If the honest answer is "this guard is defeated" or "that is a stored
energy hazard," it has to arrive before the thing that sends them toward the
machine, not underneath it.

This is a done-when condition, and it is the one non-negotiable ordering rule in
the skill.

**What counts as a safety implication.** Set `safety_flagged: true` when the
evidence shows any of these, and write which one, with its evidence, in
`safety_reason`:

- a seized or locked rotating part: spindle, chuck, bar feeder, conveyor
- a defeated, bypassed or failed guard or interlock
- stored energy: springs, counterweights, a part under load, a raised axis
- hydraulic or pneumatic pressure that has to be bled before work
- an electrical fault: a trip, a burnt smell, exposed or damaged wiring
- a fault that was cleared by restarting rather than fixed (*"ran off and
  restarted"*), now repeating

When none of these is shown, the flag is false and `safety_reason` says *"none
of the safety triggers shown"*. Never set the flag on a feeling, and never leave it off
because the diagnosis is uncertain: an uncertain stored-energy hazard is a
safety implication.

---

## Inputs

**First, find the plant setup:** from the task's own folder (never `cd` into the plugin), run
`python3 -I <this skill's folder>/../../shared/scripts/plant_setup.py find`, do its `setup_page_first` step, then read the profile at
`profile_path` and any rate at `rates_path`, per `../../shared/replies.md`.

| Input | Source | Form |
|---|---|---|
| The breakdown event | User report, or a maintenance work order | Conversation / CMMS connector or maintenance export |
| Asset record and specs | CMMS | CMMS connector, else the asset register export |
| Maintenance history and close-out notes | CMMS | CMMS connector, else the maintenance export |
| Current PM plan for the asset | CMMS | CMMS connector |
| Sensor window around the failure | Historian export to M365, scheduled or on-demand | CSV |
| Technician photos | M365, or uploaded in conversation | Images |
| Manufacturer's manual | M365 document library | PDF |
| Production context — what was running | `data-consolidate` output, or a direct MES export | `../../shared/contracts/consolidated-dataset.md` |

---

## Workflow

### Step 1 — Capture the event

Asset, time it went down, the symptom as the technician describes it, and any
fault codes the machine is showing. Take their words; do not translate a symptom
into a cause at capture.

### Step 2 — Pull the sensor window

A configurable period before the failure. **Read excursions, trends and step
changes, not just threshold breaches** — a vibration reading that climbed for six
hours without ever crossing its alarm limit is a bearing failing in plain sight.

Verify the window covers the event. If it does not, say so and do not reason
from adjacent data as if it were the event.

### Step 3 — Mine the maintenance history and close-out notes

Weight recency and symptom similarity. Search this asset, **then siblings of the
same model** — a new machine with no history is not a dead end.

**Run both searches as queries, in code, and keep what they returned.** One
filter on this asset's ID, one across every asset of the same model on the
symptom's own words. The work orders each query returned go into the figures
block (`../../shared/computed-figures.md`) by number. "This asset has eleven
prior...[truncated]

# The five evidence sources, and how to read each

A technician standing at a stopped machine has all five of these available and
time to assemble none of them. That gap is the skill.

**MTTR's largest component is usually not the repair.** It is the diagnosis —
working out what is actually wrong. Every minute spent there is a minute the
plant is not producing.

Listed in order of value, which is not the order anyone expects.

---

## 1. Free-text close-out notes — the highest-value input in the plugin

When a technician closes a maintenance work order, they write what they found in
prose:

> *"Bearing was hot, replaced, coupling was misaligned again."*

That sentence contains a diagnosis, a repair, and a recurring root cause that
nobody has acted on. It is written by the person with their hands on the machine,
it is the most honest record in the plant, and **nobody has ever aggregated it.**
It sits in a text field on a work order and is read once, by the person who wrote
it, never again.

### How to mine it

**Search this asset first, then siblings of the same model.** A machine that is
new or has thin history is not a dead end — the same model in the next bay has
been failing in the same ways for years.

**Weight by symptom similarity, then by recency.** A note describing this exact
symptom from two years ago beats a generic note from last month.

**Read what the words actually say, including the throwaway ones.** "Again" is
the single highest-signal word in a close-out note. So are "still," "same as
last time," "temporary fix," and "needs proper repair when we have time." Each
one is a technician telling you this is unresolved.

### Check for templates before citing anything

A CMMS lets a technician pick a stock close-out phrase, and many do. "Spindle
noise reported. Could not reproduce. Monitored." on five machines of three
different makes on the same day is a default, not five observations. Group the
notes by exact text and count the makes and models each group spans (model from
the asset name if the record has no model column; say so). Text shared across
makes is shown, labelled "same text on N assets — not specific to this
machine", and never cited as this asset's evidence. The same failure on
same-model siblings is cited, as a fleet pattern. Do the grouping in code and
print it, so the cited set is the same on every run over the same data.

### Report coverage honestly

Many notes are useless. "Fixed." "Repaired." "OK now." A field that exists is
not a field that says anything.

**State what fraction of the relevant history carried usable notes.** Do not
over-read a terse note into a pattern — per
`../../../shared/absent-is-not-zero.md`, an empty note is not evidence of a
simple repair.

> *"Nine prior work orders on this asset. Four have substantive close-out notes;
> five say only 'repaired' or similar. The pattern below rests on those four."*

---

## 2. The sensor window — read shapes, not thresholds

The historian logs temperature, vibration, pressure and spindle load at high
frequency. Pull a configurable period **before** the failure.

**Look for excursions, trends and step changes — not just threshold breaches.**
This is the whole point. A vibration reading that climbed steadily for six hours
and never once crossed its alarm limit is a bearing failing in plain sight, and a
threshold check reports nothing at all. Three shapes worth naming:

| Shape | Typically means |
|---|---|
| A steady climb | Progressive wear — bearing, tool, belt |
| A step change | Something discrete happened — a part let go, a setting changed, a fixture moved |
| An excursion that recovered | An intermittent fault, which is the hardest kind to catch and the most valuable to have caught |

**Verify the window actually covers the event.** If the export stops an hour
before the failure, say so and **do not reason from adjacent data as if it were
the event.** That is the highest-risk error available here.

**No sensor data at all is very common** — most assets in most plants are not
instrumented. Proceed on the other four sources and say plainly that sensor
evidence was unavailable. This is not a degraded run; it is the normal one.

---

## 3. Maintenance history

What has broken before, what fixed it, what has been replaced recently.

Weight **recency and symptom similarity** together. A part replaced last week is
relevant to a failure this week in a way a five-year-old record is not — both
because it may be the cause and because it may have been installed wrong.

**A new asset with no history falls back to the manual and to sibling assets of
the same model.** State which you used.

---

## 4. Photos — a genuine multimodal advantage

Technicians photograph what they see, and always have. Read them for:

- Visible damage, leaks, scoring, discolouration, wear patterns
- Part numbers on the failed component, which shortens the repair
- Display readings and fault codes on the machine's own panel

**Describe what is visible. Never assert a diagnosis from an unclear image.** A
blurry photo of a dark housing supports nothing, and saying so costs nothing.

> *"The photo shows fluid pooled below the left side of the housing and
> discolouration around the upper bearing cap. I can't tell from this image
> whether the fluid is coolant or hydraulic oil, and that distinction changes
> the diagnosis — worth a look."*

---

## 5. The manufacturer's manual

A PDF sitting in a document library, containing exactly what is needed and never
opened during a breakdown: troubleshooting trees keyed to fault codes,
tolerances, and specified procedures.

Match the fault code the machine is displaying to the manufacturer's own tree,
and **cite the page**. A manufacturer's stated tolerance beats an inference every
time.

---

## The citation rule

Every candidate cause carries the specific evidence behind it — including the
**specific prior work order numbers**, so the technician can read what was
actually done last time rather ...[truncated]

# What a reply holds — documents, records, memory and names

**Shared across every skill.** Four rules about what goes in front of the
person and where things are kept.

---

## Documents are printed in full; records are summarised

A **document** is what a person reads, signs or sends: the quote, the cost
sheet, the NCR, the 8D, the RFQ package, an email draft, the morning report,
the intake form. **It is printed in the reply, in full.** Saving a copy to a
file as well is fine; a file *instead of* the reply is not. The person reads
the reply, and every delimited block and outbound check lives in it.

read on a page, not in the chat. For
the bid comparison the headline is the provisional recommendation and its main
tradeoff, the exceptions are the requirements still open before an award, and

When a document is also saved as a file, and it should be wherever the person
downloads from a file card (Cowork), the file is one a plant opens without
thinking about it:

| What it is | File |
|---|---|
| A controlled document: customer quote, supplier RFQ package, NCR, escape notification, 8D, trade study memo | `.docx` |
| A table someone works in: internal cost sheet, bid comparison, ranked candidates, scrap or downtime lists | `.xlsx` |
| A report or dashboard | the HTML page, per `artifact-style.md` |
| A record (contract payload, day record, register row) | its contract's format, as below |

**Never `.txt` or `.md` for a document.** A plain-text quote reads as a draft
nobody finished, and it is what a person gets when no format is named.

- **How.** Use the session's Word or Excel skill where there is one (Cowork

  reply already holds the document.
- **The plant's template.** A controlled document keeps the structure
  `onboarding` captured. Where that example is a `.docx` in the documents
  folder, start the Word copy from that file; otherwise use a plain layout
  and keep the *template not on file* flag the document already carries.
- **What goes in which file.** The customer's file holds only what the
  sendable block holds. Internal figures (hours, rates, margin, the cost
  build-up) go in their own file, the internal cost sheet, and never into the
  customer's.
- **Names.** What it is and its reference: `quote-Q-EXAMPLE-MEDICAL-4402A-01.docx`,
  `cost-sheet-Q-EXAMPLE-MEDICAL-4402A-01.xlsx`, `NCR-2026-0141.docx`. Name each file in
  the reply.

A **record** is a handoff to another skill or a store: a contract payload (a
downtime record, a geometry estimate), a register row, a pulse day record, a
supplier bid record, a selection record, a sourcing-event row. **It is never
pasted into the reply as a raw YAML or JSON block.** A quality manager, a
buyer or an estimator should not have to read 150 lines of field names to

Instead:

1. **Save the full record** where its contract says, or to a file next to the

2. **Show a short table of the fields a person decides on**, under their

3. **If the record cannot be saved** (no write access this session), print it

The person can always ask for the raw record ("show me the YAML"). Then print

Safety first

Follow your plant's lockout procedure before anyone works on this machine. This is not a safety assessment.

Safety flagged: yes. The spindle drive tripped on SPINDLE OVERLOAD / OVERTEMP (an electrical/drive trip), and the spindle was grinding for about 20 minutes before it. The OEM page (Section 7.4) says: do not run a spindle that is grinding, and lock out the spindle drive before turning it by hand or inspecting it. The spindle nose is reported blue from heat, and the last spindle temperature reading was 52.1 °C. Do not power up the spindle or reset the alarm to "see if it runs". Every check below is done with the spindle drive locked out, except the chiller check, which does not involve the spindle.

VMC-02: breakdown diagnosis

ADVISORY: not confirmed by a technician Draft only: nothing written to any system SYNTHETIC test data

Answer

Most likely cause: spindle bearing damage or loss of preload (medium confidence). It has been getting worse for months, and the spindle chiller may have helped it along. Spindle vibration rose steadily for the whole 144-minute window, from 1.8 to 11.2 mm/s (6.22 times higher), and kept speeding up. Temperature rose from 31.0 to 52.1 °C. Coolant pressure stayed flat between 19.8 and 20.1 bar. The OEM table matches "overtemp with rising vibration" and "grinding noise" to bearing wear, bearing damage or contamination. VMC-02's own history shows the same trend: "rough at 8k" in March (MW-118), then vibration up from 1.4 to 2.1 mm/s in July (MW-140, 1.5 times higher), "told sup", and no follow-up work order in the export.

Cheapest test to tell the candidates apart, in this order, about 10 to 15 minutes in total and no parts needed:

  1. Check the chiller fluid level and flow (sight glass or flow indicator). This does not involve the spindle. If the chiller is low again, as in MW-160, that confirms candidate 2 as a contributing cause. It does not rule out candidate 1, because a low chiller does not explain the vibration rise or the grinding.
  2. With the spindle drive locked out, pull the tool holder and inspect its taper and the spindle taper for pull-out marks, fretting or scoring. If you see pull-out marks, candidate 3 (drawbar) moves up. If the holder is clean, candidate 3 moves down.
  3. With the spindle still locked out, turn it by hand (OEM check for grinding). If it feels rough, notchy or tight, candidate 1 (bearing) is confirmed. If it turns smoothly, candidate 1 is weaker and the run-out check comes next.

The next step costs more: a dial indicator run-out check at the taper (the OEM limit is under 3 µm), done with the spindle still not running. The OEM's vibration-spectrum check needs the spindle running, so do not use it here.

Sensor observation summary

The window covers the event: 7 samples from 2026-11-10 13:00 to 15:24 (-05:00). The last sample is at the alarm time. The export has no alarm thresholds, so this summary reads the shapes in the data, not alarm breaches.

  • Vibration: a steady climb that speeds up, with no single step. It never went down between samples. The rate of rise went from 0.003 to 0.825 mm/s per minute between the first and last sample pairs. This is the progressive-wear pattern (bearing). It does not look like one sudden event.
  • Spindle temperature and load climbed alongside vibration. Load rose from 42 to 71 % while the operator reported normal chips. That points to the spindle itself (friction) rather than the cut, but this is reasoning, not something the data proves.
  • Coolant pressure stayed flat between 19.8 and 20.1 bar. This is cutting-coolant pressure. The export has no chiller flow, level or temperature channel, so the sensor data neither supports nor rules out a chiller problem.

Ranked candidate causes

1. Spindle bearing damage or loss of preload (progressive wear)

Evidence

  • Sensor: vibration rose 6.22 times (1.8 to 11.2 mm/s) and kept speeding up. Temperature rose 31.0 to 52.1 °C and load rose 42 to 71 %. Coolant pressure was flat.
  • Operator: grinding noise for about 20 minutes before the alarm, with normal chips.
  • Manual, Section 7.4: "Overtemp with rising vibration" points to spindle bearing wear or preload loss, and "Grinding noise" points to bearing damage or contamination.
  • History on this asset: MW-118 (2026-03-02): "spindle sounded a bit rough at 8k, monitor". MW-140 (2026-07-08): "vib reading 2.1 mm/s at 8k (was 1.4 last yr). told sup". That is 1.5 times higher, an early warning with no corrective work order after it in the export (searched up to 2026-09-24).
  • Bluish discolouration on the spindle nose and taper is consistent with overheating near the front bearing. This comes from a written description only, with no photo, so it is not used as proof.

First check

With the spindle drive locked out, turn the spindle by hand and feel for roughness or notchiness (OEM check). If that is unclear, measure run-out at the taper with a dial indicator against the OEM limit of under 3 µm. Do not run the spindle for a vibration spectrum.

Expected fix and repair path

Replace the spindle bearings or rebuild or exchange the spindle cartridge, following the OEM procedure. Inspect the spindle taper for heat damage and regrind it if needed. After the repair, record a new baseline vibration reading at 8k. Before releasing the machine, also check the chiller (candidate 2) and drawbar clamp force (candidate 3), so the new bearings are not running with the same problems.

Cited: MW-140, MW-118.

2. Spindle chiller low flow or low fluid level (cooling), likely contributing rather than primary

Evidence

  • The alarm includes OVERTEMP, and the spindle temperature rose to 52.1 °C.
  • History on this asset: MW-160 (2026-09-23): "spindle hot after long cycle. checked chiller - low on fluid topped up. temp ok after". The chiller was topped up, but the export shows no cause for the fluid loss (leak) being found.
  • Against: the manual matches chiller problems to "Overtemp, normal vibration". Here vibration rose 6.22 times, and a chiller problem does not explain grinding. The sensor export has no chiller channel.

First check

Check the chiller fluid level and flow. This is the cheapest check of all, takes a couple of minutes and does not involve the spindle. If the fluid is low again, look for the leak.

Expected fix and repair path

Top up the chiller, find and fix the leak, and confirm flow against the OEM chiller specification (that figure is not on the excerpt supplied). If this is the only finding but the spindle still turns rough by hand, candidate 1 stands, and a low chiller probably sped up the bearing damage.

Cited: MW-160.

3. Drawbar clamp force low (tool holder not seated)

Evidence

  • The alarm includes OVERLOAD, and load rose to 71 %.
  • History on this asset: MW-131 (2026-05-19/20): "spindle alarm 2nd shift. found drawbar clamp low, adjusted belleville stack. ran ok". This is a previous spindle alarm with this exact cause. Adjusting the Belleville stack is not the same as replacing it, so it may have weakened again.
  • Bluish discolouration on the taper could also come from a loose holder fretting in the taper. A written description cannot tell this apart from bearing heat.
  • Against: the manual matches drawbar problems to "Overload with tool pull-out marks", and no pull-out marks are reported (nobody has looked yet). The vibration pattern is a smooth climb with no step. A holder letting go would more likely show a step change.

First check

With the drive locked out, pull the holder and look for pull-out or fretting marks on the holder taper. If you find marks, measure clamp force with the gauge. The OEM specification is 8.0 to 9.5 kN.

Expected fix and repair path

Replace the Belleville spring stack, not just adjust it. Set clamp force within 8.0 to 9.5 kN and inspect or replace the damaged holder. If the spindle taper is fretted, it needs regrinding.

Cited: MW-131.

The evidence does not support two candidates equally. Candidate 1 is backed by the sensor shape, the manual and two prior notes. Candidates 2 and 3 each rest on one prior note and part of the alarm text.

Cited history and coverage

There are 4 maintenance records for VMC-02 (filter asset_id == "VMC-02"), and all 4 have substantive close-out notes. All 4 mention the spindle, vibration, drawbar or chiller. The notes reuse no wording: grouping by exact text gives 5 groups, and 0 of them appear on more than one asset. Each note therefore counts as evidence about the asset it was written for.

It found VMC-03, whose record matched none of the symptom terms (MW-152 "coolant pump replaced - not related"). So no fleet pattern was found by this search. Because the model is inferred only from the name, this is not proof that same-model machines are clean.
